title: Near and Sub-Surface Damage Evolution During Cyclical Bending in Tension, and its Relation to Elongation of CP-Ti
content: Sheet metals that are processed via cyclical bending in tension (CBT) can experience remarkable increases in elongation-to-failure (ETF) compared to deformation via simple tension. The main reason for the increased ETF relates to the incremental forming during CBT, which prevents localization and subsequent failure. However, this does not appear to be the entire story. The act of bending and unbending the sheet leads to a cyclical stress state being applied towards the surfaces, potentially leading to significantly different hardening behavior and damage accumulation, compared with sheets subjected to simple tension [1]. The current study investigates damage evolution in commercial purity titanium during both simple tension and CBT processing, using X-ray computed tomography (XCT) [2]. Near-surface and through-thickness damage accumulation is compared with measurements of geometrically necessary dislocations, using high-resolution EBSD (HREBSD), and total dislocation density, from X-ray diffraction [3]. Analysis of the final fracture surface, using regular scanning electron microscopy, is also compared with the damage in the pre-fractured specimens. The results indicate a slower accumulation of damage (both in terms of void growth and dislocation accrual) near the surfaces of the sheet when processed with CBT, compared with simple tension, as hypothesized.
